doc.title: Mike Longo interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2019

title: Hearing music in his head and studying with Benny Carter's advice
summary: He writes without a piano; his first compositions were terrible until he heard unplayed music at the Jazz Workshop, and Benny Carter advised classical composition study, leading to Frank Gaskin Fields and Hall Overton.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: There’s a certain anticipation when you’ve written something on paper and you haven’t really heard it.
No I heard it when I wrote it.
You can hear it in your head?
Okay. So you’d be then surprised if something didn’t work? Is that a fair statement?

Well you might make a mistake and have to correct it during the rehearsal. But most of the time I proofread it myself and, you know, I’d check it out on a keyboard to make sure the voicings were right. But I don’t write at the piano and so I hear the music in my head. I hear the band playing. When I first — my first attempts at composition were terrible. Awful. Until I went with Dizzy. And I was playing at the Jazz Workshop in San Francisco. And I remember coming home one night to the hotel. It was one night when the band was really on, man, we were hitting it. I got to the hotel and I couldn’t go to sleep because I kept hearing the band playing. Then I said, “Wait a minute. I hear the band playing but it’s nothing we played.” So I got up and wrote down what I heard and brought it in the next day and Dizzy played it. And that’s how my — and then I started to realize oh, you’ve got to have an inner voice that you listen to. And then I went to — Dizzy got invited to Benny Carter, you remember Benny, invited Dizzy to dinner up in Baldwin Hills so Dizzy took me as a guest. So I asked Benny, I said, “Man we were playing out here maybe two months at a time, can I study arranging with you?” He says, “You don’t want to study arrangements, you want to study classical composition. When you get back to New York find you a good classical composition teacher.” So I came back and I studied two years of counterpoint with Frank Gaskin Fields. This was an African-American cat. He had no talent for jazz. He was like Mendelssohn or something. This guy was a genius. And he taught me counterpoint with no textbook, just out of his head. And he wouldn’t take more than five dollars a lesson. And he had a bunch of guys. And he would tell the guy, when I’d play my stuff, he’d say, “See that’s what music’s all about, right there.” And he would say, “It’s not worth more than five dollars, it ain’t nothing but the facts.” And so I studied. He died man. And then I studied with Hall Overton for two years, composition.
